title: Bidirectional Dijkstra in Chicago: Route Engine ⚡
description: Watch how Bidirectional Dijkstra shrinks the search space by expanding from both start and goal until the frontiers meet. In this Chicago grid visualization, you’ll see why route planners get faster at shortest-path scale.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional Dijkstra: How Modern Route Planners Scale — Inside high-scale navigation engines, visualized ⚡ 

In this Chicago (West Loop) run, two priority-queue frontiers move at once: one from the start (forward graph) and one from the destination (reverse graph). Each step expands the lowest tentative distance, and the moment the frontiers “touch,” we can stitch the best meeting point into the global shortest path.

What you’re seeing (technical but practical):
• Two Dijkstras → effectively cuts explored nodes when the true path is far.
• “Meet in the middle” → stop early instead of expanding the whole reachable space.
• Complexity intuition → same worst-case logic, but dramatically better in typical road-network geometries.

Takeaway: Bidirectional search is a scalability pattern—don’t just optimize constants, reduce the search frontier itself.

Debate question: In real route engines, would you rather bidirectional search, A* with landmarks, or hybrid heuristics—and why?
